passages.title: The Book from Allah and the powerless idols
passages.tafsir:
This surah opens by naming the source of the Book — it comes from Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise — and by stating that the heavens and the earth were made with truth and for a specified term. It then turns on the one claim that stands against all of this, the claim that there are other gods beside Allah, and demands the evidence for it.

**What holds these six ayat together** is a single chain of reasoning that runs from source to consequence. Ayah 2 names *who* is speaking. Ayah 3 states that the world He made was not made in idle play, and that it is running to a fixed term — so a warning about it is not idle talk. Ayah 4 puts the opposing claim on trial and demands proof for it. Ayah 5 delivers the verdict on those who cling to it anyway. Ayah 6 shows where that road ends: on the Day when mankind are gathered, with the "gods" turning on the very people who worshipped them.

## Ayah 1: the two letters

The surah begins with **Ḥā Mīm** — given as two Arabic letters rather than as a word. The commentary before us offers no interpretation of them; Ibn Kathir moves straight from them to the announcement of ayah 2. That restraint is worth noticing and worth imitating. Where the sources are silent, the honest thing is to be silent with them, and to let the letters hand us over to the sentence that follows.

## Ayah 2: where the Book came from

*The revelation of this Book is from Allah — the Almighty, All-Wise.*

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is informing us that He has revealed the Book to His servant and Messenger Muhammad ﷺ — "may Allah's blessings be upon him until the Day of Judgement."

Note what the ayah leads with. Not the content of the Book, not its rulings, not its promises — its **origin**. That is what is settled first.

Then Allah names Himself with two attributes, and Ibn Kathir unfolds them: Allah describes Himself as being **of unimaginable glory** (*al-ʿAzīz*, the Almighty), **possessing ultimate wisdom in His statements and actions** (*al-Ḥakīm*, the All-Wise). Wisdom, on Ibn Kathir's own gloss, governs both what Allah says and what Allah does — both His statements and His actions.

## Ayah 3: a world made in truth, and running on a clock

*We created not the heavens and the earth and all that is between them except with truth, and for a specified term.*

Two claims about reality, each one dense.

**"Except with truth"** — Ibn Kathir's gloss is a single sharp phrase: *not in idle play and falsehood*. The heavens and the earth are not a diversion and not a toy. There is a truth built into their making.

**"And for a specified term"** — Ibn Kathir: *for a fixed and specified duration that will not increase or decrease*. The appointment is already set, and nothing moves it forward and nothing pushes it back.

Put the two together and you have the ground on which the whole warning stands: a world made with truth, and a term that will neither increase nor decrease.

**"But those who disbelieve, turn away from that whereof they are warned."** Ibn Kathir explains: the disbelievers are *distracted from what is intended for them*. Then he presses the point — Allah has indeed revealed to them a Book and sent to them a Messenger; yet they obstinately turn away from all of that. And so, he concludes, "they will soon realize the consequence of their behavior."

Notice the diagnosis Ibn Kathir gives. Their problem is not that the evidence never arrived. A Book came. A Messenger came. The failure he names is one of attention: they are *distracted* from what is intended for them, and they turn away obstinately. That is a far more ordinary and a far more dangerous condition than open denial, and it is worth every believer asking whether some version of it has crept into his own days.

## Ayah 4: the argument put on trial

*Say: "Think you about all that you invoke besides Allah? Show me what have they created of the earth? Or have they a share in the heavens? Bring me a scripture prior to this or some trace of knowledge, if you are truthful!"*

Ibn Kathir notes that the command **"Say"** is directed at these idolaters who worship others besides Allah. What follows is not abuse and not mockery — it is a demand for evidence, and it is the intellectual centre of the passage.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out the logic with unusual clarity. The polytheists' claim that other gods exist is refuted here **by demanding a proof to substantiate it** — because no claim can be accepted, neither rationally nor according to religious principles, unless it is proved by concrete evidence. And rather than answering one argument, the ayat deal with all possible types of argument at once. Maʿārif classifies them into **three types**, and shows the ayah negating each in turn.

**1. The rational argument.** *"Show me what they have created of the earth; or have they a share in the heavens?"* Maʿārif states that this phrase negates any rational argument in their favour. Ibn Kathir reads "show me what they have created of the earth" as: *show me the place that they have independently created from the earth* — point to one patch of ground that is theirs by making. And on "or have they a share in the heavens?" he is emphatic: they are not partners in anything, in the heavens or on earth. **They do not own even the thin membrane covering a date's pit.** The dominion and the control belong to Allah alone, Exalted is He.

Ibn Kathir then turns the questions on the worshippers themselves: *How then would you worship others or join them as partners with Him? Who guided you to that? Who called you to that? Did He command you to do it, or is it something that you suggested yourselves?* The last question is the trap closing. If Allah never commanded it, then it was something they suggested themselves.

**2. The argument from revealed scripture.** *"Bring me a scripture prior to this."* Ibn Kathir: bring a book from among the Books of Allah revealed to the Prophets **that commands you to worship these idols**. Maʿārif states the principle underneath the demand — in any matter concerning Allah, no one can be an authority except Allah Himself, and His statements are established either through the divine books, such as the Torah, the Injīl, or the Qur'an, or through the sayings of the prophets He sent. So: produce the book revealed before the Qur'an that allows idol-worship.

**3. The argument from a prophet's word.** *"Or some trace of knowledge."* Maʿārif reads this as the second branch of authority: if you cannot bring any revealed book to prove the validity of idol-worship, then at least put forward some authentic saying of any prophet that proves your contention. The Arabic word is **atharah** — Maʿārif explains that it is an infinitive in the sense of *reporting*, and that **ʿIkrimah and Muqātil** explained it to mean a dictum of a prophet. Maʿārif notes that this explanation is taken from the Tafsir of Qurtubi and is the one accepted by most exegetes; other views on the ayah exist, but Maʿārif judges them neither well-established nor in full harmony with the textual structure, and so the majority of the exegetes did not adopt them. As the author adds: Allah knows best.

Ibn Kathir gives a slightly broader gloss of the same phrase — *some clear evidence justifying this way you have chosen* — and then records that **some recited it** as *atharah min ʿilm*, "or something inherited from knowledge," that is, true knowledge you have inherited from anyone before you. He cites **Mujahid** on the phrase: "Or anyone who has inherited any knowledge."

**"If you are truthful!"** Ibn Kathir's summary of the challenge is devastating in its brevity: *you have absolutely no evidence for that — neither textual (from revelation) nor rational.* And Maʿārif draws the conclusion: if you can do neither — no revealed book, no saying of a prophet — then your words and deeds are totally misguided.

There is a lasting lesson in the *method* here, quite apart from idols. Maʿārif's principle is stated plainly: no claim is accepted, rationally or religiously, without concrete evidence to support it; and in any matter concerning Allah, no one is an authority except Allah Himself, through His revealed books or through the sayings of the prophets He sent. Beyond that, sincerity is no substitute for evidence.

## Ayah 5: the most astray of all

*And who is more astray than those who invoke besides Allah others who will not answer them until the Day of Resurrection, and who are unaware of their invocations to them?*

The form of the question — *who is more astray than…* — is a way of saying there is no one. Ibn Kathir states it plainly: no one is more misguided than those who invoke idols instead of Allah, **asking them for things that they cannot give**, until the Day of Judgment.

Then he lays out why, and each clause removes another possibility. The idols are *unaware of what he asks*. They **can neither hear, see, nor act**. And the reason is not mysterious: they are **inanimate, senseless stones**.

Sit with the picture the ayah draws. A person in need — really in need — pours out his heart. Words, tears, hopes, promises. And on the other end there is nothing: no hearing, no seeing, no acting. "Until the Day of Resurrection" tells you how long this goes on.

## Ayah 6: the day the false gods turn on their worshippers

*And when mankind are gathered, they (false deities) will become their enemies and will deny their worship.*

The final ayah of the passage moves the scene to the gathering of mankind, and it is the cruellest turn of all. The beings a person spent his life honouring do not merely fail him there — they become his **enemies**, and they **deny the worship he gave them**.

Ibn Kathir brings two other passages of the Qur'an alongside it. First, Allah's saying: *"They have taken gods beside Allah, that they might give them dignity. No! They will deny their worship of them, and will be opponents to them"* (19:81–82). His comment is exact — **they will betray them when they need them the most**. The stated purpose of taking these gods was that they might give them dignity. At the moment of greatest need, they betray.

Second, the words of Ibrāhīm al-Khalīl, peace be upon him: *"You have taken only idols besides Allah! The love between you is only in the life of this world. On the Day of Resurrection, you shall disown each other and curse each other, and your abode will be the Fire, and you shall have no helpers"* (29:25). Ibrāhīm names the limit on false attachments — *only in the life of this world*. What looked like love and belonging turns, on that Day, into mutual disowning and mutual cursing.

## Living it

Read as one unit, these six ayat put three questions to the reader.

**Where does your conviction come from?** The passage names the source of the Book in ayah 2, and in ayah 4 it demands that the other side produce a source of their own — a revealed book, or the saying of a prophet. Maʿārif's principle is portable: in any matter concerning Allah, no one is an authority except Allah Himself, through His books or through the prophets He sent. A claim about Allah with nothing behind it is not piety.

**Where does your calling go?** Ayah 5 defines the deepest misguidance as calling on those who cannot answer. Duʿāʾ — supplication — is the act at the centre of this ayah, and Ibn Kathir's reason the idols cannot receive it is that they can neither hear, see, nor act, being inanimate, senseless stones. The dominion and the control, he says, belong to Allah alone, Exalted is He. So the question the ayah leaves with a believer is a simple one: who do you turn to first when something goes wrong?

**What will still be standing when mankind are gathered?** Ayah 6 asks you to look at what you love, and to ask whether it will stand with you on that Day or against you. Ibrāhīm's words draw the line — the love in those attachments is *only in the life of this world*.

And behind all of it, ayah 3: the heavens and the earth were not created in idle play and falsehood, and their term is fixed and will neither increase nor decrease. The warning is real, and it is timed.

passages.title: Charges against the Qur'an and their answers
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat put the accusations of the Makkan idolators on trial. The Qur'an quotes their charges — *this is plain magic*, *he made it up*, *if it were any good we would have got there first*, *this is an ancient falsehood* — and answers them, ending with the Qur'an's own credentials in ayah 12. What holds the passage together is a single question the disbelievers refuse to face: **what if this really is from Allah?**

## The setting: a demand for evidence

Just before this, in ayah 4, the idolators were asked for evidence for the gods they call on besides Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the demand was made exhaustively — no claim, rationally or religiously, is accepted without concrete evidence — and that three kinds of proof were ruled out in turn: a rational proof ("Show me what they have created of the earth; or have they a share in the heavens?"), a proof from revealed scripture ("Bring to me a book revealed before this one" — any earlier scripture permitting idol-worship), and a proof from prophetic authority ("or a trace of knowledge"). That last phrase turns on *athārah*, an infinitive in the sense of *reporting*, explained by ʿIkrimah and Muqātil as a saying handed down from a prophet; Maʿārif notes this is Qurṭubī's explanation and the one most exegetes accept. If you can bring neither, Maʿārif concludes, "then your words and deeds are totally misguided."

So the idolators arrive at ayah 7 with no proof of any of the three kinds. What follows is not an argument but an accusation.

## Charge one: "This is plain magic" (ayah 7)

Note the framing Ibn Kathīr gives it: it is *when the clear Ayat of Allah are recited to them* that they say this. He glosses *siḥrun mubīn* as "simple magic," and his verdict on the charge is blunt: in this statement of theirs "they have lied, invented a falsehood, went astray and disbelieved."

Ibn Kathīr heads this whole stretch of the sūrah "Refuting Claims of the Idolators about the Qur'an and the Messenger ﷺ," and opens it by saying it concerns "the disbelief and rebellion of the idolators." The charge of magic belongs to that category — not a finding they reached, but a posture they took.

## Charge two: "He fabricated it" (ayah 8)

The second charge is aimed at the Prophet ﷺ personally: *iftarāhu* — he invented it and attached it to Allah. Ibn Kathīr notes plainly that "they are referring to Muḥammad ﷺ." The reply Allah dictates does not begin by protesting innocence. It begins with the consequences:

> "Say: If I have fabricated it, still you have no power to support me against Allah."

Ibn Kathīr unpacks the logic: *if I lie against Allah and falsely claim that He sent me when He actually had not, then He would punish me with a severe punishment — and no one on the earth, you or anyone else, would be able to protect me from Him.* He links this to Allah's words in Sūrat al-Jinn, "None can protect me from Allah, nor would I find a refuge except in Him; my duty is only to convey from Allah and deliver His Messages" (72:22–23), and to the terrible warning of Sūrat al-Ḥāqqah: if he had invented sayings against Us, "We surely would have seized him by the right hand, then We would have cut off his life artery, and none of you could withhold Us from punishing him" (69:44–47).

A forger fears exposure by people; the Prophet ﷺ is told to say that his fear is of Allah alone — and that if he were a forger, the very audience accusing him could not shield him for a moment.

Then: **"He knows best of what you say among yourselves concerning it"** — the private conversations behind the public sneer are already known. And **"Sufficient is He as a witness between me and you."** Ibn Kathīr calls this "a severe threat, intimidation and warning for them."

**And then the door opens.** The ayah ends on two names of Allah — *al-Ghafūr, al-Raḥīm*, the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Merciful. Ibn Kathīr reads this as deliberate encouragement to repent and turn to Allah: *despite all of this, if you turn back and repent, Allah will accept your repentance, pardon you, forgive you, and have mercy upon you.* He points to the identical move in Sūrat al-Furqān, where the same slander ("legends of the ancients, dictated to him morning and afternoon") is answered with "It has been sent down by the One Who knows every secret within the heavens and the earth. Truly, He is ever Forgiving and Merciful" (25:5–6).

## "I am not a new thing among the Messengers" (ayah 9)

This is the Prophet ﷺ himself, told to state what they had evidently assumed. *Mā kuntu bidʿan min al-rusul.* Ibn Kathīr: *I am not the first Messenger who ever came to the world; rather, Messengers came before me. I am not an unprecedented incident that should cause you all to reject me and doubt my being sent to you. Indeed, Allah has sent before me all of the Prophets to various nations.*

The answer is historical — this is how Allah has always dealt with humanity. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that ayah 12 closes this loop: Mūsā (peace be upon him) came before as a messenger, and the Torah was revealed to him, a book the Jews and Christians all accept.

## "Nor do I know what will be done with me or with you"

**A moment from the Prophet's life.** Ibn Kathīr records, via Imam Aḥmad, the report of Kharijah bin Zayd bin Thābit from Umm al-ʿAlāʾ — a woman of the Anṣār who had pledged loyalty to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. When the Anṣār drew lots to take in the Muhājirūn, her household received ʿUthmān bin Maẓʿūn. He fell ill in her house; they nursed him until he died and wrapped him in his garments for burial. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ came in, and she said, "O Abū al-Sāʾib! May Allah have mercy on you. I bear witness that Allah has indeed honoured you." He ﷺ asked, "How do you know that Allah has honoured him?" She said, "I do not know — may my father and mother be ransoms for you!" He ﷺ said: "As for him, certainty has reached him from his Lord, and I surely wish well for him. But by Allah, even though I am Allah's Messenger, I do not know what will happen to me." She said, "Never will I claim a person to be pious after this." The matter distressed her; she slept and saw in a dream that ʿUthmān owned a running water spring. She told the Prophet ﷺ, and he said, "That was his good deeds." Ibn Kathīr notes al-Bukhārī recorded this ḥadīth but Muslim did not.

Hope is voiced; the verdict is not.

**What the scholars draw from it.** Ibn Kathīr says this and similar texts show that it is not allowed to declare of a specific person that he will enter Jannah, except those whom Allah or His Messenger ﷺ distinctly named — he lists the Ten, Ibn Sallām, al-Ghumayṣāʾ, Bilāl, Surāqah, ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAmr bin Ḥarām (Jābir's father), the seventy reciters killed near the Well of Maʿūnah, Zayd bin Ḥārithah, Jaʿfar and Ibn Rawāḥah, may Allah be pleased with them all.

**Does the Prophet ﷺ know the unseen?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats this carefully, and the answer turns on the very next clause: *"I only follow what is revealed to me."* Read as an exception to what precedes, the sense is: *I know nothing except what comes to me by waḥy* (revelation). Maʿārif summarises Imam Ḍaḥḥāk's explanation — the Prophet ﷺ obtains knowledge of unseen matters only through revelation, and has no knowledge of unseen things not revealed to him, whether about himself, about the believers and disbelievers among his people, or about this world or the Hereafter; whatever he ﷺ said about the unseen was obtained through waḥy. It adds that the Qur'an itself declares he was blessed with knowledge of innumerable unseen things — "These are some reports from the unseen which We reveal to you" (11:49) — and that the details of the Hereafter, Hell, Paradise and the reckoning are in the Qur'an, while many details of future events are in authentic aḥādīth from him ﷺ. His knowledge of the unseen is neither all-encompassing like Allah's nor independently obtained.

Maʿārif then quotes the author of *Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī*: he believes the Prophet ﷺ did not leave this world until he was blessed by waḥy "with such a knowledge about Allah, His attributes, and about all those things the knowledge of which could be meritorious, that no other in the whole universe has ever been blessed with" — while unawareness about trivial worldly affairs, such as what particular individuals do at their homes, in no way reduces his excellence. Maʿārif also records a point of adab: respect for the Prophet ﷺ means one should not say that he did not know the Unseen, but rather that Allah gave him such vast knowledge of unseen matters as was not given to any other prophet.

Maʿārif reports a genuine difference honestly: some exegetes held that the negation concerns only unseen affairs of *this world*, not the Hereafter — a view Maʿārif attributes to Qurṭubī — since the Prophet ﷺ told very clearly about the Hereafter that the believer would go to Paradise and the disbeliever to Hell. Maʿārif suggests they reached this by not reading "I only follow what is revealed to me" as an exception to the previous sentence.

**A related question of ordering.** ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that this ayah was followed in revelation by "That Allah may forgive for you your sins of the past and future"; ʿIkrimah, al-Ḥasan and Qatādah said it was abrogated by that verse. They mention that when the latter was revealed, one of the Muslims said, "Allah has declared what He will do for you. But what will He do for us?" — and Allah revealed, "That He may admit the believing men and the believing women to Gardens under which rivers flow." Ibn Kathīr adds that what is confirmed in the Ṣaḥīḥ is that the believers said, "May you enjoy that, O Allah's Messenger! But what do we get?"

**"And I am but a plain warner."** Ibn Kathīr: his warnings are obvious to every person of sound intellect and reason — no claim to independent knowledge, no claim to control outcomes, only the office of conveying clearly.

## The hinge: "What if it really is from Allah?" (ayah 10)

Ibn Kathīr paraphrases: *what do you think Allah will do to you if this Book I have come to you with is actually revealed to me from Him for me to convey — and you disbelieve in it and deny it?*

Then the witness: *a witness from the Children of Israel has testified to something similar and believed, while you rejected it in arrogance.* Ibn Kathīr explains "something similar" as the previous Scriptures revealed to the Prophets before him, which all testify to the Qur'an's truthfulness and authenticity and had prophesied, well in advance, about things similar to what it conveys. The one who testified did so, in Ibn Kathīr's words, "due to his realization that it was the truth," while you "arrogantly refused to follow it." Masrūq's comment cuts to the bone: **"That witness believed in his Prophet and Book, while you disbelieved in your Prophet and Book."**

Who is the witness? Ibn Kathīr holds the wording is general — any witness — including ʿAbdullāh bin Salām and others, noting that the ayah was revealed in Makkah before he accepted Islam. He compares it with 28:53 and with 17:107–108, where those given knowledge fall on their faces in prostration. At the same time he reports from Saʿd (may Allah be pleased with him): "I have not heard Allah's Messenger ﷺ say about anyone walking on the surface of the earth that he is of the people of Jannah — except for ʿAbdullāh bin Salām," and that this ayah was revealed concerning him — recorded, Ibn Kathīr says, in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs and an-Nasāʾī, with Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatādah, ʿIkrimah, as-Suddī, ath-Thawrī, Mālik bin Anas and others saying the same. He reconciles the two: since the sūrah is Makkan and ʿAbdullāh bin Salām embraced Islam in Madīnah, the ayah functions as a prophecy of what was to come.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it in the same spirit: the verse names no particular scholar and does not specify whether the testimony had already been given or was still to come; in effect it sounds a warning that if such a situation has arisen or should arise, one had better worry about saving oneself. Maʿārif links it to "Is it not a proof for them that the knowledgeable of the Children of Israel recognise him?" (26:197) — the deniers are ignorant of their own books, while many scholars of Banī Isrāʾīl, finding his prophethood and its signs mentioned there and witnessing those signs, came to believe in him.

Maʿārif also draws ayat 8 and 10 together: the forgery charge collapses first because a false claimant to prophethood would be eliminated by divine punishment in this world, so that ordinary people are saved from his fraudulent claims; and second, if you will not accept that argument, at least do not overlook the possibility that the claim is correct and the Book really is from Allah — in which case, with one of their own learned men testifying and believing, what will their end be, and how severe a punishment will they deserve?

## Charges three and four: snobbery, and "an ancient falsehood" (ayah 11)

*"Had it been any good, they would not have preceded us to it."* Ibn Kathīr identifies who "they" were: Bilāl, ʿAmmār, Ṣuhayb, Khabbāb, may Allah be pleased with them, and others like them — the weak, the male servants and the female servants. The pagans said this "only because they thought that they held a high status with Allah, and that He took special care of them," and by that "they made a great and obvious error." He cites "Thus have We tried some of them with others, that they might say: Is it these whom Allah has favoured from among us?" (6:53).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names the mechanism: **arrogance and pride pervert the human intellect.** An arrogant person makes his own opinions and deeds the criteria for right and wrong; whatever he dislikes he judges worthless, and everyone who values it stupid — "while he himself is stupid." Maʿārif reports, from a narration reproduced by Ibn Mundhir and others (via Maẓharī), that this verse was revealed about Zunayrah, a slave-girl of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him) who had embraced Islam while he was still a disbeliever. She used to be beaten and threatened by him so that she might give up Islam; and the disbelievers of Quraysh would say that had this faith been a good thing, a worthless woman like Zunayrah would not have preceded them in embracing it.

**A striking reversal.** Ibn Kathīr observes that the position of Ahl al-Sunnah waʾl-Jamāʿah is the contrary of theirs — of any act or saying not reported from the Companions: "It is an innovation. If there was any good in it, they would have preceded us in doing it, because they have not left off any of the good characteristics except that they hurried to perform them." The same form of words is falsehood when the measure is worldly rank, and truth when the measure is the Companions' devotion.

**"This is an ancient falsehood."** Ibn Kathīr: an old lie — they mean the Qur'an has been quoted and taken from the ancient people, thereby belittling both the Book and its followers. He calls this clear arrogance, and cites the Prophet's ﷺ definition of arrogance: **rejecting the truth and belittling people.** The two halves fit the two halves of ayah 11 exactly.

## The answer in full: what this Book actually is (ayah 12)

The passage closes with description, and every word answers something that was said:

- **"And before this was the Scripture of Mūsā"** — Ibn Kathīr: the Tawrāh. So the Prophet ﷺ is not "a new thing," and neither is the Book.
- **"as a guide (imām) and a mercy"** — the earlier revelation is honoured, not dismissed.
- **"And this is a Book confirming"** — Ibn Kathīr: confirming that which came before it of the previous Books. Not an ancient falsehood, but a continuation of the same true line. As Maʿārif puts it, Mūsā (peace be upon him) and the Torah are themselves witnesses that Muḥammad ﷺ is Allah's Messenger and the Qur'an is Allah's Book — exactly the argument of ayah 10.
- **"in the Arabic tongue"** — Ibn Kathīr: it is eloquent and clear. Not magic, not muddled incantation; clear speech in their own language.
- **"to warn those who do wrong, and as glad tidings for the doers of good"** — Ibn Kathīr: a warning to the disbelievers and glad tidings for the believers.

## Living it

**Answer the accusation, then leave the door open.** The model reply in ayah 8 argues the point squarely and ends on Allah's forgiveness and mercy — which Ibn Kathīr reads as an encouragement to repent and turn to Allah. Winning the argument is not the goal; the person is.

**Guard against the sentence in ayah 11.** "If it were any good, people like *that* wouldn't be doing it" is a judgement about status masquerading as a judgement about truth — worth remembering whenever we dismiss something because of who is drawn to it. Maʿārif's diagnosis is worth keeping close: arrogance perverts the intellect, and the man who makes his own taste the measure of good calls everyone else stupid while being stupid himself.

**Hold hope and fear together.** The Prophet ﷺ said of a Companion who had died that he wished well for him but did not know what would happen even to himself. That is not despair — the same context promises Gardens beneath which rivers flow for believing men and women. It is the posture of a servant who leaves the verdict with Allah and gets on with the deeds.

passages.title: Steadfastness, and the son who thanks his parents
passages.tafsir:
This passage folds the whole of Islam into two short statements: a creed held firmly until death (ayat 13–14), and a life lived beautifully towards the two people who carried you into the world (ayat 15–16). Both end in the same place — the Garden.

**Where we are in the surah.** Ayah 12 has just said the Qur'an came "to warn those who do wrong, and as glad tidings for the doers of good." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that ayat 13–14 complete that: after the warning to the unjust comes the good news of success and reward for the virtuous Muslims.

## "Our Lord is Allah," and then they stood firm

Ayah 13 is famously compact. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says that in this one sentence "all the basic faith and virtuous deeds required by Islam have been comprehensively referred to with great eloquence." The confession *rabbunā Allāh* — "Our Lord is Allah" — is, in itself, the whole of faith. And *thumma istaqāmū* — "and then they stood firm" — includes holding on to that confession till death, as well as carrying out all its obligations. Both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān point the reader to the parallel discussion in Surah Ha Mim As-Sajdah (41:30) for what *istiqāmah* (steadfastness) means.

**Two fears removed.** "No fear shall come upon them, nor shall they grieve." Ibn Kathir draws a fine distinction: *no fear* concerns their future; *nor shall they grieve* concerns what they have left behind. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it the same way: freedom from anxiety and suffering to come, and the dispelling of grief and sorrow over past sufferings. We are anxious forward and sorrowful backward; the promise reaches both directions.

**And then made permanent.** Ayah 14: "It is they who will be the residents of Paradise, staying there forever." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that this second ayah exists precisely to give "glad tidings of the permanence and continuity of this matchless comfort."

**"A reward for what they used to do."** Ibn Kathir's whole comment on this tying of Paradise to deeds is: they "are a cause for their attaining the mercy and their being engulfed by it — and Allah knows best." The deeds are named as the cause; what the servant arrives at, and is surrounded by, is mercy.

## Why parents, right here?

The turn in ayah 15 can feel abrupt: from creed and Paradise to a pregnant mother's exhaustion.

**Ibn Kathir's answer** is that this is the Qur'an's usual style: after mentioning that one must confess Allah's Oneness, worship Him with sincerity, and remain upright in obeying Him, Allah follows it with instructions regarding parents. He notes that the two appear together in many places of the Qur'an, and cites two: "Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and that you be dutiful to your parents" (17:23), and "Be grateful to Me and to your parents. Unto Me is the final destination" (31:14). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that many verses of the Qur'an, in various surahs, bear witness to this style.

**Qurtubi's answer**, which he reports from Qushairi, reads the sequence as a kind of solace for the Prophet ﷺ. He should keep calling people to faith and *tawḥīd* (Allah's Oneness) and not be disheartened when some refuse — because men, by nature, are of diverse characteristics, and some of them do not refrain even from ill-treatment of their parents. If a person can be that hard towards the one who bore him, his rejection of a messenger is less discouraging.

## The weight of two words: *waṣṣaynā* and *iḥsān*

Ayah 15 opens: *wa waṣṣaynā al-insāna bi-wālidayhi iḥsānā*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up both key words. *Waṣiyyah* here does not mean gentle advice; it means an **emphatic order**. And *iḥsān* is not merely "being nice" — it is doing good, behaving beautifully, and includes **service, obedience, respect and reverence**: your hands, your compliance, your manner, and your inward posture towards them. Ibn Kathir's gloss runs the same way — Allah has commanded that we treat them well and show compassion towards them.

**The setting in which the command came down.** Ibn Kathir records — from Abu Dawud At-Tayalisi, from Saʿd bin Abi Waqqas, may Allah be pleased with him — that Saʿd's mother said to him: "Hasn't Allah commanded that you obey your parents? Then I will not eat any food or drink any drink until you disbelieve in Allah." She stubbornly abstained from eating and drinking, until they had to open her mouth with a stick. Then this ayah was revealed. Ibn Kathir notes it was also recorded by Muslim and the Sunan compilers, except for Ibn Majah. The command that a person treat his parents beautifully was sent down in the middle of exactly that scene.

## The mother's account, item by item

**"His mother carried him in hardship."** Ibn Kathir spells out what the mother suffers because of her child: fatigue, sickness, vomiting, heaviness, distress, and the other forms of hardship that pregnant women suffer.

**"And she delivered him in hardship."** The same word again — now the pains of labour and their severity.

**A distinction in the Arabic.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the vowel: *kurh* is the toil one has to endure for some reason, while *karh* is the toil one undertakes under compulsion from someone else. The word here is *kurh* — hardship borne, not hardship imposed by another.

**"His bearing and his weaning is thirty months."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this clause too describes the mother's hardship: after the pregnancy and the severe labour pains she gets no respite, because the infant's natural food is in her body and she must nurse him.

**Why only the mother is mentioned.** The command in the first half of the ayah is to both parents — so why does the second half speak only of her? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the reason plainly: her hardships are *unavoidable*, and no child can be born without them. A father, by contrast, does not necessarily suffer hardship in bringing up and educating a child if he can afford to pay somebody else for those services. That, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is why the Prophet ﷺ gave the mother more rights than anybody else, reporting his words: "Do good to and serve your mother, then your mother, then your mother, then your father, then the near relatives and then those who come after them."

## Thirty months, and a woman's life at stake

**The deduction.** ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, read this ayah alongside "his weaning is in two years" (31:14) and "the mothers suckle their children two complete years" (2:233). Thirty months total, minus twenty-four months of suckling, leaves six. Therefore the **minimum period of pregnancy is six months**. Ibn Kathir calls this a strong and valid conclusion, approved by ʿUthman and a number of the Companions.

**The case.** Ibn Kathir records, from Muhammad bin Ishaq bin Yasar from Baʿjah bin ʿAbdullah Al-Juhani, that a man of Juhaynah married a woman of the same tribe and she delivered a baby after six months. The husband went to ʿUthman, may Allah be pleased with him, who summoned her. As she was getting dressed, her sister began to cry. She asked her: "Why do you cry? By Allah, no one has ever approached me of Allah's creation except him. So let Allah decree for me as He wills." ʿUthman commanded that she be stoned. ʿAli heard of it, came to him and said: "What are you doing?" ʿUthman said: "She delivered after six months! Can this ever happen?" ʿAli said: "Don't you read the Qur'an?" — and laid out the arithmetic of the ayat. ʿUthman said: "By Allah, I did not see that! Bring the woman back." But they found she had already been killed. Baʿjah adds that the child turned out to resemble his father beyond any doubt — his father said, "By Allah! This is my son without any doubt" — and that Allah afterwards afflicted the father, for his false accusation, with a skin abscess in his face that kept eating him up until he died. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays the incident from Qurtubi in a milder form — ʿAli advised ʿUthman against the decision, ʿUthman accepted the argument, and the order was cancelled. Either way, the correction came from nothing but careful attention to the Book.

**Ibn ʿAbbas's refinement.** Ibn Kathir records from him: if a woman delivers after nine months the baby needs only twenty-one months of suckling; after seven months, twenty-three; after six months, two full years. The Qur'an gave the combined figure of thirty months, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, without defining each period separately, precisely because the two periods move against each other.

**Where the jurists agree and differ.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports all the jurists of the Ummah unanimous that the minimum period of pregnancy can be six months. On the maximum they differ, since the Qur'an gives no ruling about it: Abu Hanifah held two years; from Malik there are different narrations of four, five or seven years; Shafiʿi held four, as did Ahmad according to the more recognised reports from him. On suckling — which governs the rules of fosterage — the maximum is two years according to the majority of jurists (Malik, Shafiʿi, Ahmad, and Abu Yusuf and Muhammad of the Hanafi school), and this is also the dictum of ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbas, with ʿAli and Ibn Masʿud reported to the same effect. Only Abu Hanifah is quoted for two and a half years, which the majority of the Hanafi school understand to mean that a weak child who takes no food but his mother's milk after two years may be suckled a further six months. The prevalent Hanafi verdict follows the majority, though Maulana Thanawi advised, as a matter of precaution, that fosterage be presumed if a child was suckled within six months past the age of two. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also notes the reverse asymmetry: the minimum suckling period is left undefined, because some women produce no milk at all, some have their milk dry up within a few months, and some babies do not take to it or are harmed by it.

## Forty years old, and a man finally prays

**"Until, when he reaches his full strength and reaches forty years."** The lexical meaning of *ashudd* is strength. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the same word in Surah al-Anʿam (6:152) was explained to mean the age of puberty, and that Ibn ʿAbbas explained it as reaching the age of eighteen. The scholars then divided: Shaʿbi and Ibn Zayd took *ashudd* as puberty and "reaches forty years" as a separate, later stage; Hasan Basri held both phrases to have the same meaning, with "reaching forty" explaining what attaining full strength is. (Qurtubi records both.)

Ibn Kathir explains "forty" as the point at which a person's intellect, understanding and patience reach the level of maturity — and adds that it has also been said that usually one will not change his ways once he reaches the age of forty. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same: experience shows that the ethical manners and habits one is accustomed to at forty become permanent in one's character and are not easily changed. That is why the du'a in this ayah lands where it does.

**The prayer, phrase by phrase.**

- *Rabbi awziʿnī* — "My Lord, grant me the power and ability." Ibn Kathir glosses *awziʿnī* as **"inspire me."** The man does not claim gratitude; he asks to be enabled to have it.
- *"…grateful for Your favour bestowed upon me and upon my parents"* — the favour he names covers both himself and them.
- *"…and that I may do righteous deeds that please You"* — Ibn Kathir notes this means **in the future**: the deeds still to come.
- *"…and make my offspring good"* — his offspring and descendants, says Ibn Kathir. Reminded of what his parents bore for him, he turns and asks for the generation after him.
- *"Truly I have turned to You in repentance, and truly I am one of the Muslims"* — Ibn Kathir draws the instruction directly: this **contains an instruction for anyone who reaches forty to renew his repentance and turn to Allah with strong resolution**.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a report from ʿUthman that the Prophet ﷺ said: when a believer reaches forty, Allah becomes lenient in taking account of his deeds; at sixty He gives him the ability to turn to Him constantly; at seventy all heavenly beings begin to love him; at eighty Allah lets his virtues stand and his sins be erased; and at ninety Allah forgives his sins, past and future, and authorises him to plead for the forgiveness of his family. (Attributed there to Ibn Kathir and the Musnad of Ahmad; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this obviously concerns a believer who has lived avoiding sins and in accordance with the Shariah.)

## Whose story is this?

**A particular man.** Tafsir Mazhari held that the whole description relates to Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him — noting that the Qur'an gives it all in the past tense, in a style indicating a particular person and a particular event that had already happened. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays the narration of Ibn ʿAbbas reproduced by Qurtubi: when the Prophet ﷺ travelled to Syria for trade financed by Khadijah he was twenty, and Abu Bakr, who was with him, was eighteen — having "reached his maturity," in the Qur'an's words. What he witnessed of the Prophet's ﷺ qualities on that journey made him an ardent admirer, and he kept his company thereafter. When the Prophet ﷺ reached forty and was blessed with prophethood, Abu Bakr was thirty-eight, and became the first adult male to embrace Islam. When he became forty he prayed this very prayer — and Allah accepted it: he was given the ability to purchase and set free nine slaves who had embraced Islam and were being tortured mercilessly by their masters, and his petition for his progeny was accepted in that all his children embraced Islam. Of all the noble Companions, only Abu Bakr has the distinction that he, his parents, and his offspring all embraced Islam and had the honour of being Companions.

There is an objection: his father Abu Quhafah embraced Islam only after the conquest of Makkah, yet the whole of this surah is Makkan. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two answers. Some exegetes held these ayat to be Madani, which leaves no room for the question. Or, if the verse was revealed in Makkah, the inclusion of his parents in the supplication was by way of praying that they be blessed with Islam — the "favour bestowed" on them being the worldly benefits they were already enjoying, with Abu Bakr praying that they be granted the ability to offer gratitude for those favours by embracing Islam (Ruh-ul-Maʿani; this last clarification from Mufti Muhammad Taqi Usmani).

**Anyone at all.** Ibn Kathir adopted the other explanation: the verse does not refer to any particular person, and the specifics — attaining maturity, reaching forty — stand by way of example, teaching that at forty a person should have due care for correcting himself and his family, and that his effort for the Hereafter should take precedence over all his other concerns.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān will not let the difference become an escape hatch: even if a verse of the Qur'an is revealed about a particular person or a particular incident, the rule it lays down remains generally applicable to all.

## What Allah does with such a life

Ayah 16 is the settlement. Ibn Kathir identifies who "those" are: **those who repent to Allah, turn back to Him, and rectify their shortcomings through repentance and seeking forgiveness**.

**"We accept from them the best of what they did."** Not the average of their deeds — the best. And Ibn Kathir's summary is striking: many of their errors will be forgiven, and Allah will accept from them **a modest amount of deeds**.

**"Among the dwellers of Paradise."** That is Allah's ruling concerning them, as He has promised those who repent and turn to Him — "a promise of truth that they had been promised." The passage closes where ayah 14 closed: creed and conduct arriving together at the same door.

**A Companion's use of this ayah.** Ibn Kathir reports the narration of Muhammad Ibn Hatib that he was once with ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, along with some others who were blaming ʿUthman for some wrongdoings. ʿAli said: "ʿUthman was one of those people about whom Allah has said: *Such are the people from whom We accept the best of what they did, and overlook their evils… among the people of Paradise, according to the true promise that was made to them.* I swear by Allah that ʿUthman and the companions of ʿUthman were examples of this verse." He repeated it three times. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites this as an indication that the sense of the verse is general.

## Living it

**Hold the line.** Saying "our Lord is Allah" is the easy half. *Thumma istaqāmū* — holding on to it till death, and carrying out all its obligations — is the half being rewarded.

**Serve them, and know what it cost.** *Iḥsān* here means service, obedience, respect and reverence — and the ayah insists you know the price paid: carried in hardship, delivered in hardship, nursed for months after. And note *waṣiyyah*: this is not gentle advice but an emphatic order.

**Do not let forty pass unmarked.** Renew your repentance and turn to Allah with strong resolution. And the prayer of ayah 15 is not only about oneself: it names parents and offspring together, asking that gratitude and goodness run through all three generations at once.
