## What this passage is doing

These four ayat hold up the exact mirror-image of the child described just before them. Ibn Kathir frames it precisely: in the previous ayat Allah mentions the dutiful offspring who supplicate for their parents and treat them with kindness, and describes the success and salvation He has prepared for them — and *here*, connected to that same discussion, He places the situation of the wretched offspring who are undutiful toward their parents. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it the same way: the previous ayah laid down the order to serve and obey parents; this one announces the punishment for one who maltreats them and is impertinent to them.

What holds the four together is a widening lens. Ayah 17 is a scene inside one house — a child, two parents, one argument. Ayah 18 pulls back to show that this person is not an isolated case but one name among nations that have already passed. Ayah 19 pulls back further, to the ranking of *everyone* by deed. And ayah 20 lands on a single sentence spoken to the disbelievers as they are exposed to the Fire, a sentence about how they spent their lives.

## The scene in ayah 17

The child says **أُفٍّ لَكُمَا** — rendered in translation as *"Enough with you!"* and *"Fie upon you both!"* Ibn Kathir keeps the focus on the word itself: as for the saying "Uff" in this ayah, **it is a general description applying to anyone who says it to his parents.**

And what has provoked it? They are calling him to faith. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān highlights this as what sharpens the offence: the verse announces punishment for one who maltreats his parents and is impertinent to them **especially when they are calling him towards Islam and virtuous deeds, because rejecting their call is a double sin.**

His objection is a denial of resurrection: **أَتَعِدَانِنِي أَنْ أُخْرَجَ** — "Do you promise me that I will be raised?" Ibn Kathir glosses أُخْرَج simply: *resurrected*. And his evidence is what he can see around him — **وَقَدْ خَلَتِ الْقُرُونُ مِنْ قَبْلِي**, "when generations before me have passed." Ibn Kathir unpacks the unspoken half of the sentence: generations of people have already passed away, **and none of them has ever returned to tell what happened to them.** That is his whole case. Nobody comes back; therefore, he concludes, nothing happens.

**Meanwhile, the parents.** The Qur'an gives them one of the most moving verbs in the passage: **وَهُمَا يَسْتَغِيثَانِ اللَّهَ** — the two of them *invoke Allah for help*. Ibn Kathir explains what they are asking for: **they ask Allah to guide him.** They have run out of arguments, so they turn to the One who turns hearts. And to their son they say **وَيْلَكَ آمِنْ** — "Woe to you! Believe! Verily, the promise of Allah is true." Their alarm is not for themselves; it is for him.

His reply closes the door: **مَا هَٰذَا إِلَّا أَسَاطِيرُ الْأَوَّلِينَ** — "This is nothing but the legends of the ancient." Old stories. Folklore. The tenderest appeal a human being can receive — a parent begging on his behalf — is answered with a shrug at "legends."

## Was this about one particular man? A famous and instructive dispute

Ibn Kathir is emphatic on the first point: the "Uff" here **is a general description applying to anyone who says it to his parents.** He then addresses a claim that circulated — that the ayah was revealed about ʿAbdur-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr — and rejects it outright as **weak and rejected**, for a plain historical reason: ʿAbdur-Rahman embraced Islam *after* this was revealed, his adherence to Islam was excellent, and he was among the best of his contemporaries.

Where did the claim come from? Ibn Kathir traces it, and the story is worth telling because it shows how a verse of the Qur'an can be picked up and used as a political weapon.

**Al-Bukhari recorded** from Yusuf ibn Mahak: Marwan ibn al-Hakam was governor of the Hijaz, appointed by Muʿawiyah ibn Abi Sufyan. Marwan delivered a speech in which he mentioned Yazid ibn Muʿawiyah and urged the people to give a pledge of allegiance after his father. ʿAbdur-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr said something to him in response, upon which Marwan commanded his men: "Arrest him!" But ʿAbdur-Rahman entered ʿAishah's house, and they were not able to capture him. Marwan then said: "This is the one about whom Allah revealed, *'But he who says to his parents: Uff to you! Do you promise me that I will be raised — when generations before me have passed?'*"

From behind the curtain, ʿAishah responded: **"Allah did not reveal any Qur'an in our regard — the children of Abu Bakr — except for the declaration of my innocence."**

**In another report recorded by An-Nasa'i**, Muhammad ibn Ziyad reported that when Muʿawiyah was soliciting people to pledge allegiance to his son, Marwan declared: "This follows the tradition of Abu Bakr and ʿUmar." On hearing this, ʿAbdur-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr said: "Rather, this is the tradition of Heraclius and Caesar." Marwan responded: "This is the one about whom Allah revealed, *'But he who says to his parents: Uff to you!'*" When that was conveyed to ʿAishah, she said: "Marwan is lying! By Allah, that was not revealed about him. If I wish to name the person meant by it, I could." In that same report she added a rebuke concerning Marwan's own lineage — that Allah's Messenger ﷺ had placed a curse on Marwan's father, al-Hakam ibn Abi al-ʿAs, when Marwan was still in his loins.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān summarises the upshot cleanly: Marwan's claim **has been contradicted by Sayyidah ʿAishah, as narrated in the Sahih of Bukhari.** The fact of the matter is that the verse is general in sense, and **there is no correct narration which states this verse to hold true for a particular person.**

Two things sit inside this episode. First, a political ruler quoted the Qur'an at an opponent to shame him, and a woman of knowledge behind a curtain corrected the record. What a verse was revealed about is settled by evidence, not by who holds the pulpit. Second — and this is why Ibn Kathir bothers with it at all — the door of this ayah is left open, and it is open toward *us*. It is not a verdict on a dead man. It is a description of a type.

## The grammar that shows it is a type (ayah 18)

Ibn Kathir points to a beautiful detail. Ayah 17 begins with a **singular** relative pronoun: **وَالَّذِي قَالَ** — "But he who says." Then ayah 18 answers it with a **plural** demonstrative: **أُولَٰئِكَ** — "*Those* are those against whom the Word has justified." Placing "Those are" after "But he who says," Ibn Kathir says, **confirms that the latter is a general description of a type of people, including all those who fall under that description.**

Al-Hasan and Qatadah both defined that type in one line: **"This applies to the disbelieving, sinful person who is undutiful to his parents and who denies resurrection."** Three things braided together — rejection of faith, contempt for parents, denial of the Last Day.

**حَقَّ عَلَيْهِمُ الْقَوْلُ** — "the Word of torment has justified against them." And the company named is sobering: **فِي أُمَمٍ قَدْ خَلَتْ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ مِنَ الْجِنِّ وَالْإِنْسِ** — among previous generations of jinn and mankind that have passed away. Ibn Kathir: this indicates that all such people will be among **their likes and their peers** among the disbelievers.

Then the verdict: **إِنَّهُمْ كَانُوا خَاسِرِينَ** — "Verily, they are ever the losers." Ibn Kathir specifies the loss: they **lose themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection.** Read that against ayah 17 and it stings. The one who sneered at the two people praying for him is told that on that Day the loss is total — it takes in his family, and it takes in himself.

## Everyone placed at their exact level (ayah 19)

**وَلِكُلٍّ دَرَجَاتٌ مِمَّا عَمِلُوا** — "And for all, there will be degrees according to that which they did." Commenting in the flow of these ayat about the deniers, Ibn Kathir reads it as **degrees of punishment for each of them according to what they did** — the Fire is not one flat sentence; it is graded.

That the ranking runs both ways is captured in the words of **ʿAbdur-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam**, quoted by Ibn Kathir: **"The levels of the Fire descend, and those of Paradise ascend."** One image, two directions. Every soul finds the rung its own deeds cut for it — some climbing, some sinking, none misplaced.

**وَلِيُوَفِّيَهُمْ أَعْمَالَهُمْ وَهُمْ لَا يُظْلَمُونَ** — "so that He might fully recompense them for their deeds, and they will not be wronged." Ibn Kathir explains the guarantee: Allah **will not be unjust to them even in the amount of a speck of dust or less.** No one on that Day will be able to say *I was given worse than I earned.*

## The sentence spoken at the Fire (ayah 20)

**وَيَوْمَ يُعْرَضُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا عَلَى النَّارِ** — the Day those who disbelieve will be *exposed* to the Fire. And there they are told: **أَذْهَبْتُمْ طَيِّبَاتِكُمْ فِي حَيَاتِكُمُ الدُّنْيَا وَاسْتَمْتَعْتُمْ بِهَا** — "You received your good things in the life of the world, and you took your pleasure therein."

Ibn Kathir notes the tone: this will be said to them **by way of blame and reprimand.** It is not information; it is the closing of the ledger in front of them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the accounting behind that sentence. The disbelievers are being told that they **had already been awarded** delights, luxuries and enjoyment in the worldly life for whatever good deeds they had done there, and **now there is nothing left for them in the Hereafter.** It is known from this verse, Maʿārif says, that the good deeds of disbelievers have no worth in the Hereafter due to lack of faith — yet Allah does not leave them unrequited: He compensates them **in this world.** The riches and wealth, honour and dignity that disbelievers enjoy in this world are all recompense for their good deeds, benevolence, sympathy and truthfulness. And then a crucial guardrail: **this rule does not apply to believers** — a believer who receives delights, riches and wealth in this world is *not* thereby deprived of his right in the Hereafter.

**The punishment matches the crime.** Ibn Kathir says of **فَالْيَوْمَ تُجْزَوْنَ عَذَابَ الْهُونِ** — "Today, you will be recompensed with the torment of *extreme humiliation*" — **بِمَا كُنْتُمْ تَسْتَكْبِرُونَ فِي الْأَرْضِ بِغَيْرِ الْحَقِّ** — "because you were arrogant upon the earth without a right" — **وَبِمَا كُنْتُمْ تَفْسُقُونَ** — "and because you used to rebel against Allah's command" — that **their punishment will be of a type comparable to their deeds.** They enjoyed themselves, were arrogant in their denial of the truth, and were involved in sinning and disobedience; so Allah punishes them with **extreme humiliation, disgrace, severe pains, continued sorrow, and positions in the terrible depths of Hell** — may Allah protect us from all of that. Arrogance answered by humiliation; indulgence answered by loss.

Look back at ayah 17 and the arrogance was already visible: not merely disbelief, but contempt — "Uff", "legends of the ancient." The whole passage is one arc from a sneer to the humiliation that answers it.

## Living it

**Fear the reprimand more than you enjoy the comfort.** Ibn Kathir records that the Commander of the Faithful, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, gave up many of the joys of food and drink and refrained from them, saying: **"I am afraid of being like those whom Allah has reproached and condemned by saying, *'You received your good things in the life of the world, and you took your pleasure therein.'*"** That ʿUmar took this ayah personally — while leading the Muslims — should stop us from filing it under "verses about disbelievers."

**Good things can be spent in the wrong currency.** Abu Mijlaz said: "Some people will *lose* good deeds that they had in the worldly life, and they will be told, *'You received your good things in the life of the world.'*" A deed cashed out for comfort and reputation here may leave nothing on deposit there.

**Hold this world loosely.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān titles this section *Incentive for avoiding worldly delights and luxuries*, and reasons: since the punishment stated here is because of their being engrossed in worldly enjoyments, the Prophet ﷺ, his noble Companions and the Tabiʿin — the generation that came after the Companions and learned from them — had made it a habit to avoid worldly enjoyments, as is evident from their lives. It reports that the Prophet ﷺ charged Sayyidna Muʿadh, when sending him to Yemen, to keep on avoiding the luxuries of this world; and it relays from Sayyidna ʿAli that the Prophet ﷺ said that one who is happy with Allah giving him scanty sustenance finds Allah also happy at his meagre deeds (relayed in Maʿārif from Mazhari, from al-Baghawi). Balance this, as above, with Maʿārif's own guardrail: worldly provision is not itself a disqualification for a believer. The danger is being *engrossed* — treating this life as the payout rather than the passage.

**And the household in ayah 17.** Two things this passage asks of us there. If you are the child: the word "Uff" is enough to earn a mention in the Qur'an, and it costs nothing to swallow it — especially when what your parents are urging on you is Islam and virtuous deeds, where rejecting their call is, as Maʿārif says, a double sin. If you are the parent of someone who has turned away: notice that the parents in this ayah do exactly two things — they speak the truth plainly ("Believe! Verily, the promise of Allah is true") and they invoke Allah for help. Ibn Kathir tells us what they are asking for: **they ask Allah to guide him.** Their child's answer, in the ayah, does not change; their own standing before Allah is what the Qur'an has preserved. That is a father's and mother's work.

passages.title: Hūd warns 'Ād and the destroying wind
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat tell, in compressed form, the story of Hud (peace be upon him) and his people 'Ad: a warner sent to his own kin, a people who dared him to bring on the punishment, and a cloud on the horizon that they welcomed as rain and that turned out to be the very thing they had asked for. The passage moves in one arc — a warning delivered, a dare thrown back, a messenger's restrained answer, a mistaken joy, and then the silence of empty houses.

Ibn Kathir opens his comment on the passage by naming its purpose: Allah says this **consoling His Prophet ﷺ** over the rejection he was meeting from those who opposed him among his people. The Makkans who mocked him were not the first to mock; a people who came before them had done the same, and their empty dwellings were the reply.

## A brother, not a stranger

The Qur'an does not say "remember Hud." It says *"And remember the brother of 'Ad."* Ibn Kathir explains that this refers to Hud, peace be upon him, whom Allah sent to the first people of 'Ad, who inhabited Al-Ahqaf.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why he is described as their **brother** — for two reasons at once: firstly, because he belonged to their own tribe, and secondly, because he was their well-wisher as a brother is. And the Qur'an's own wording keeps him inside the tribe: he warns *his people*. Ibn Kathir notes that it was to them — his own people — that Hud said, *"truly, I fear for you the torment of a mighty Day."*

There is a beautiful trace of this Qur'anic title in the Sunnah. Under the chapter heading "He who supplicates should first mention himself," **Ibn Majah** recorded that Ibn 'Abbas narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> **يَرْحَمُنَا اللهُ وَأَخَا عَادٍ**
> *"May Allah have mercy on us and the Brother of 'Ad."*

The Prophet ﷺ used the Qur'an's own name for Hud, and the scholars placed the report under a lesson about du'a: begin with yourself, then include others.

## Al-Ahqaf: a place you could go and find

*Al-Ahqāf* is the plural of *ḥiqf*. Ibn Kathir reports that the early authorities differed over exactly what a *ḥiqf* is: according to **Ibn Zayd** it means a sand dune, while according to **'Ikrimah** it means a mountain or a cave. **Qatadah** said: "We were informed that 'Ad was a tribe in Yemen. They dwelt among sand (hills), and overlooked the sea in a land called Ash-Shihr." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes the nation as living in valleys surrounded by long, curved sand dunes — which is what the Arabic *aḥqāf* names.

Why does the Qur'an bother to give the address? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers: special reference is made to these dunes **so that one could find out their place, if he so wishes, when travelling to their localities.** This is not a fable told from nowhere. It is a ruin with coordinates.

That geography matters for the Makkan audience. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that the people of 'Ad were in Yemen, to the **south** of Makkah, while the towns of Thamud and of the people of Lut (peace be upon him) lay to the **north**, on the way the people of Arabia travelled to Syria — which is why the Qur'an speaks of such settlements as being "around you." Destroyed nations lay on either side of them, and the Makkans passed the evidence on their trade routes.

Ayah 21 adds that *warners had already passed on before him and after him.* Ibn Kathir explains this to mean that Allah had sent Messengers and warners to the towns surrounding the land of 'Ad. He connects it to Allah's words, *"And We made it a deterrent punishment for those who were present and those who succeeded them"* (2:66), and to *"I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt that struck 'Ad and Thamud. (That occurred) when the Messengers had come to them from before them and after them (saying): 'Worship none but Allah'"* (41:13–14).

Note what the message itself is, in every case: **"Worship none but Allah."** Before any law, before any detail, the warners came with the worship of Allah alone. That is precisely the quarrel that follows.

## The dare, and the answer it received

Their reply has two halves, and both are revealing.

**First:** *"Have you come to delude us from our gods?"* Ibn Kathir glosses the Arabic *li-ta'fikanā* — rendered "to delude us" or "to turn us away" — as meaning **"to prevent us"** from our gods. What they voice is not an argument that their gods are true, but resentment at being pulled away from them.

**Second:** *"Then bring us that with which you threaten us, if you are one of the truthful!"* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān underlines the horror of it: **they themselves demanded that Allah's punishment be brought upon them.** Ibn Kathir explains that they sought to hasten Allah's torment and punishment **believing that it would not happen** — the demand was a taunt. He links it to Allah's words, *"Those who do not believe in it seek to hasten it"* (42:18). Impatience for the punishment is itself a symptom of not believing in it.

Hold on to that sentence, because ayah 24 will hand it back to them word for word.

Hud's reply separates three things cleanly, and it is a model of restraint.

**"The knowledge (of that) is only with Allah."** Ibn Kathir renders Hud's meaning: *Allah knows best about you. If you deserve the punishment to be hastened, He will do that to you.* Hud does not pretend to a timetable he was not given. The *when* belongs to Allah alone, and a truthful messenger says so rather than manufacturing a date to win an argument.

**"And I convey to you that wherewith I have been sent."** Ibn Kathir continues Hud's words: *as for me, my duty is to deliver my message to you.* Delivery is the whole of the assignment.

**"But I see that you are a people given to ignorance."** Ibn Kathir explains the Arabic *tajhalūn* here to mean: *you have no comprehension or understanding.*

## The cloud they were glad to see, and the wind inside it

Now the scene turns on a single word, *fa-lammā* — "then, when…" The argument is over; the sky answers.

They see it as *'āriḍan* — rendered "a dense cloud" — *approaching their valleys*. Ibn Kathir explains that when they saw the punishment coming towards them, **they thought it to be clouds full of rain**, and that this made them **happy and joyful, because they had a drought and needed rain**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same: the punishment was sent in the form of a cloud that appeared to be benign, and they were happy to see it in the hope that it would bring them rain.

This is the most frightening detail in the passage. The disaster arrived wearing the face of a mercy they had been longing for. The last thing the Qur'an records them saying is a glad announcement of rain.

Then Allah cuts across their sentence: *"Nay, but it is that which you were asking to be hastened — a wind wherein is a painful torment."* Ibn Kathir points out the exact echo: this is the torment that you called for when you said, *"Bring to us what you promise us, if you should be of the truthful."* Their own dare is quoted back to them at the moment of its fulfilment.

*Tudammiru kulla shay'* — *destroying everything.* Ibn Kathir qualifies it precisely: destroying **every part of their land that could normally be destroyed.**

*Bi-amri rabbihā* — *by the command of its Lord.* Ibn Kathir's gloss: **it had Allah's permission to do that.** This is the theological spine of the whole story. The wind is not a blind force of nature and not a rival power; it acts by Allah's permission, and even in the act of annihilation the Qur'an calls Allah *its Lord*. Ibn Kathir compares this with Allah's words, *"It spared nothing that it reached, but blew it into broken spreads of rotten ruins"* (51:42) — meaning, like something dilapidated or decrepit.

*"So they became such that nothing could be seen except their dwellings!"* Ibn Kathir: **all of them were destroyed, and none of them were spared.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the point of the surviving houses — nothing was left except their empty homes, which **remained as a sign for those who might learn a lesson.** The buildings outlived the builders.

The passage closes with the rule the story was told to establish: *"Thus do We recompense the criminal people."* Ibn Kathir states its force plainly — **this is Our judgement regarding those who reject Our Messengers and disobey Our commands.** Not a one-off event; a judgement, and the Makkans were standing inside it. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes how the following ayat press this home: in ayah 26, that those nations were much more powerful and well-established than the people of Makkah, and their power and strength was of no use to them against Allah's punishment; and in ayah 28, that the false gods they believed to be their patrons could not save them, since those gods were coined only by their false imagination and had no real existence at all.)

Both commentaries note that the full account is given elsewhere — Ibn Kathir says he has previously mentioned the destruction of the people of 'Ad in both Surat Al-A'raf and Surah Hud, and so there is no need to repeat it here; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to Surah Hud (11:50) and calls the mention here a brief reference. It is a reminder, not a retelling.

## From the Sunnah: how the Prophet ﷺ looked at a cloud

The most striking application of this passage comes from the Prophet ﷺ himself, preserved in several narrations of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her.

**Imam Ahmad** recorded from her that she said: "I never saw Allah's Messenger ﷺ fully laughing so that I would see his uvula. He would only smile." She added that when he ﷺ saw clouds or wind, that would reflect on his face as discomfort. She asked him: "O Allah's Messenger! When the people see clouds, they become happy, hoping that they bring them rain. But I notice that when you see them, displeasure appears on your face." He ﷺ replied:

> *"O 'A'ishah! What would guarantee to me that they do not bring punishment? Some nations had been punished with wind. On seeing the punishment approaching them, a nation once said: 'This is a cloud bringing us rain.'"*

This is also recorded by **Al-Bukhari and Muslim.**

**Imam Ahmad** also recorded that 'A'ishah said that when Allah's Messenger ﷺ saw clouds on any of the horizons, he would leave whatever he was doing — **even if he was in prayer** — and say:

> **اللّٰهُمَّ إِنِّي أَعُوذُ بِكَ مِنْ شَرِّ مَا فِيهِ**
> *"O Allah! I seek refuge with You from any harm that it contains."*

If Allah removed those clouds, he would praise Allah; and if rain fell, he would say:

> **اللّٰهُمَّ صَيِّبًا نَافِعًا**
> *"O Allah! Make it pouring and beneficent."*

**Muslim** also recorded in his Sahih from 'A'ishah that when the wind blew, Allah's Messenger ﷺ would say:

> **اللّٰهُمَّ إِنِّي أَسْأَلُكَ خَيْرَهَا وَخَيْرَ مَا فِيهَا وَخَيْرَ مَا أُرْسِلَتْ بِهِ، وَأَعُوذُ بِكَ مِنْ شَرِّهَا وَشَرِّ مَا فِيهَا وَشَرِّ مَا أُرْسِلَتْ بِهِ**
> *"O Allah! I ask You of its good, the good that it contains, and the good with which it has been sent. And I seek refuge in You from its evil, the evil that it contains, and the evil with which it has been sent."*

She added that if the sky became cloudy his colour would change; he would exit, enter, come, and go — and when it rained, his anxiety would be relieved. When 'A'ishah noticed that, she asked him about it, and he ﷺ said:

> *"O 'A'ishah! It could be like what the people of 'Ad said: (Then, when they saw it as a dense cloud approaching their valleys, they said: 'This is a cloud bringing us rain!')"*

He was quoting ayah 24 about the sky over his own head.

## Living it

**Read the weather the way the Prophet ﷺ read it.** 'Ad looked at an approaching sky and saw only what they wanted; the Prophet ﷺ looked at the same kind of sky and remembered that a wind moves *by the command of its Lord*. The believer's response is neither superstition nor indifference, but the du'as above — asking for the good in it, seeking refuge from the evil in it — with praise when the clouds pass and a prayer for beneficial rain when it falls.

**Never dare Allah.** Warners had come to 'Ad before and after; they answered the warning by demanding the punishment as proof. Ibn Kathir's note is worth keeping: they sought to hasten it *believing it would not happen* — hastening the punishment is what people do when they do not really believe in it.

**Learn Hud's job description.** Convey clearly, say plainly that the knowledge of the timing is only with Allah, and stop there. Anyone who invites others to Allah — a parent, a friend, a teacher — has, as Hud put it, the duty to deliver the message, and no licence to threaten on Allah's behalf with a schedule Allah never disclosed.

**Do not mistake a favourable-looking sign for approval.** What arrives may be a mercy or may be a torment; the cloud over 'Ad looked exactly like the rain they had prayed for. That is why the Prophet ﷺ met every cloud with a du'a rather than a conclusion.

passages.title: Their strength and idols availed them nothing
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are one continuous argument, addressed by Allah to the people of Makkah about the nations He destroyed before them. Ibn Kathir renders the sweep of it in a single breath: *"And indeed We had firmly established them with that wherewith We have not established you! We also gave them hearing, vision, and hearts. But their hearing, vision, and hearts availed them nothing since they used to deny the Ayat of Allah, and they were completely encircled by that which they used to ridicule (26) And indeed We have destroyed towns round about you, and We have shown (them) the signs in various ways so that they might return (27) As for those whom they had taken for gods besides Allah, as the means of approach to Him, why then did they not aid them? Nay, but they vanished completely from them. And that was their falsehood, and what they were fabricating (28)."*

Read as one unit, the passage takes away three things a person might lean on: strength (26), the excuse of not having been shown (27), and the patrons he imagines will step in for him (28). Nothing is left standing at the end of ayah 28 except Allah.

## The setting

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that these verses are meant to remind those who rejected the Messengers of the severe punishments faced by earlier peoples who had rejected the messengers sent to them. Special reference is made to ʿĀd, the people of Sayyidnā Hūd (ʿalayhi al-salām), who is described as their "brother" — firstly because he belonged to their tribe, and secondly because he was their well-wisher, as a brother is. That nation lived in valleys surrounded by long, curved sand dunes, called in Arabic *Aḥqāf*; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that these dunes are singled out so that anyone who wishes can find their places when travelling to those localities.

The earlier verses of the sūrah supply the background in brief: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that in verse 22 that people themselves demanded Allah's punishment be brought upon them, and in verse 24 it came as a cloud they were happy to see, hoping for rain, which in fact carried a violent wind that destroyed everything and left nothing but their empty homes as a sign for those who might learn a lesson. That is the case being referred back to when ayat 26–28 turn to the living listener.

## "Established in a way We have not established you"

Ibn Kathir puts the opening of ayah 26 in Allah's own voice: *"We have granted the earlier nations wealth and offspring in the worldly life. That which We granted them, We did not give you anything similar or close to it."*

Notice how sharp that is. It is not that the destroyed nations and the people of Makkah were roughly comparable and one edged the other out. What was given to those nations, Ibn Kathir says, was not given to these listeners in any similar or even close measure. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the same point at verse 26: the infidels of Makkah are reminded that those nations were much more powerful and well-established than the people of Makkah — and still their power and strength was of no use to them against Allah's punishment.

That is the whole logic of the comparison. If greater strength bought no reprieve, on what calculation does lesser strength buy one?

## Faculties given, signs clarified, and still denied

Allah then names what else those nations were given: *samʿan wa abṣāran wa afʼidatan* — hearing, vision, and hearts. These are the very instruments by which a human being takes in guidance: sound reaches the ear, evidence reaches the eye, and the heart is where it is weighed and acted on.

And the verdict: *fa-mā aghnā ʿanhum* — their hearing, their vision and their hearts availed them nothing at all. The reason is stated immediately, and it is not a defect in the equipment: *idh kānū yajḥadūna bi-āyāti-llāh* — "since they used to deny the signs of Allah."

Ayah 27 completes this half of the picture from Allah's side. *Wa ṣarrafnā al-āyāt* — "and We have shown them the signs in various ways" — which Ibn Kathir glosses simply: *"We explained and clarified them."* And the purpose is stated openly: *laʿallahum yarjiʿūn* — "so that they might return."

Put the two ayat side by side and the case closes itself. The faculties were given. The signs were explained and clarified. The stated aim was that they should turn back. Nothing was withheld at either end — not the capacity to receive, not the clarity of what was sent. What failed was neither the gift nor the message but the response to it. A faculty is worth what it is used for, and these were used to deny.

There is a quiet warning here for anyone who prides himself on being sharp, well-informed, well-read. Those nations were not short of faculties or of clarified signs. They were short of submission.

## Encircled — and the ruins round about you

The other half of the passage is what arrived. Ayah 26 ends with *wa ḥāqa bihim mā kānū bihi yastahziʼūn* — "and they were completely encircled by that which they used to ridicule." Ibn Kathir explains the meaning: they were encircled by the torment and exemplary punishment that they had denied and whose occurrence they had doubted.

Sit with that picture. What closed around them was not something foreign to them. It was the very thing they had made light of. Their mockery had a shape, and that shape came and surrounded them from every side. And Ibn Kathir does not leave the lesson in the past tense — he turns it directly on the reader: *this means, you listeners must beware of being like them lest a punishment similar to theirs strikes you in this life and the Hereafter.*

Ayah 27 then makes the encirclement geographical: *"And indeed We have destroyed towns round about you."* Ibn Kathir says plainly that this is addressed to the people of Makkah, and lists the nations who disbelieved in the Messengers and who lived around Makkah:

- **ʿĀd**, who were at al-Aḥqāf in Ḥaḍramawt near Yemen
- **Thamūd**, whose dwellings were between Makkah and ash-Shām (Greater Syria)
- **Sabaʼ**, who were in Yemen
- **the people of Madyan**, who were on the route and passage to Ghazzah (Western Palestine)
- **the people of Lūṭ**, who dwelt by the lake — the Dead Sea — which they used to pass by on the way to Jordan

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why the word is "around": the towns of Thamūd and of Sayyidnā Lūṭ (ʿalayhi al-salām) were in the way of the people of Arabia while they travelled to Syria, to the north, while the people of ʿĀd were in Yemen, towards the south of Makkah — hence the words, "around you."

So the two ayat rhyme. In ayah 26 the punishment encircles the deniers; in ayah 27 the evidence of it encircles the listeners. These were not stories from an unreachable elsewhere. Ibn Kathir's list is a list of places, some of them on the very road travelled north to Syria. The listeners were standing in the middle of a ring of consequences, and the ayah names the purpose of that ring: *so that they might return.* The ruins are not displayed to gloat. They are displayed as an invitation while returning is still open — the same note struck in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's account of ʿĀd, whose empty homes were left standing as a sign for those who might learn a lesson.

## The gods who were not there

Ayah 28 removes the last support. *Fa-law-lā naṣarahum alladhīna ittakhadhū min dūni-llāhi qurbānan ālihah* — "As for those whom they had taken for gods besides Allah, as the means of approach to Him, why then did they not aid them?"

The wording states the idolaters' own theology in their own terms: these were taken as gods besides Allah *as the means of approach to Him*. That was the claim — that the idols brought their worshippers closer to Allah. The ayah does not argue with the theory. It simply asks what the theory delivered. Ibn Kathir puts the question as a test: *did they help them when they were in the greatest need for them?*

The answer comes in Allah's own words: *bal ḍallū ʿanhum* — "Nay, but they vanished completely from them." Ibn Kathir: *rather, they completely left them alone when they needed them the most.* The one moment those gods were counted on to be present was the one moment they were absent.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the reason without softening it: the false gods, believed by them to be their patrons, could not save them from the torment they faced, because they were coined only by their false imagination, having no real existence at all. This is worth pausing on, because it explains the failure rather than merely reporting it. It is not that help was requested and refused. There was never anyone there. The relationship was one-sided from the first day.

The passage then closes: *wa dhālika ifkuhum wa mā kānū yaftarūn* — "And that was their falsehood, and what they were fabricating." Ibn Kathir glosses *ifkuhum* as "their lie," and *mā kānū yaftarūn* as meaning that they fabricated lies by taking them as gods, and that they lost and failed in their worship of them and their reliance upon them. Then he closes as the scholars do at the edge of what can be known: *and Allah knows best.*

Two things are named in that closing verdict, and both matter: the worship itself, and the reliance placed upon it. It was in both that they lost.

## Living it

**Measure gifts by what they were used for.** Ayah 26 does not ask how much hearing, sight and understanding a person was given. It asks what they *availed* him. The faculties are a gift, and the reckoning is on their use.

**Do not take mockery lightly.** Ibn Kathir reads ayah 26 as a direct instruction to the listener: beware of being like them, lest a punishment similar to theirs strike you in this life and the Hereafter. What a person makes light of is precisely what this ayah says can close around him.

**Look at the ruins you pass.** The signs were placed around the people of Makkah, on roads they travelled, and were explained and clarified so that they might return. Every believer has his own version of these: a funeral attended without thought, a collapse watched without reflection. The ayah says they are put there on purpose.

**Audit what you actually rely on.** Ayah 28's question — where were they when you needed them? — settles every claim about a patron at the moment of crisis. Anything treated as a guaranteed rescue that displaces reliance on Allah faces the same test, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's verdict stands: what has no real existence cannot save anyone. The mercy sitting in the middle of this passage is that the audit can be done now, while returning is still open, rather than at the moment when the encirclement has already closed.

passages.title: The jinn who heard the Qur'an and believed
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat tell a single story: Allah turned a party of jinn toward His Messenger ﷺ while he was reciting, they listened, they believed, and they went straight back to their own people as warners — and ayat 30–32 are their sermon, quoted word for word. What holds the passage together is that quoted speech: the whole scene is built so that we overhear creatures we cannot see arguing for the Qur'an in front of their own nation.

Placed where it is, the passage is also an argument aimed at Makkah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that the preceding ayat have been condemning the disbelievers' arrogance and its ruinous results; now the people of Makkah are put to shame — even the jinn, prouder and more haughty than you, had their hearts softened by a single hearing of the Qur'an and submitted, while you, given more sense and understanding than they, will not believe.

## The night the sky was shut

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the incident of the jinn listening to the Qur'an and then embracing faith is stated in authentic ahadith, and it is worth telling properly, because it explains why the jinn were on that road at all.

Imam Ahmad and the famous Imam, Al-Hafiz Abu Bakr Al-Bayhaqi in his book *Dala'il An-Nubuwwah*, both record from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him) that at that time the devils had been prevented from eavesdropping on the news of the heavens, and burning flames attacked them whenever they tried to listen. When they went back to their people and were asked what had happened to them, they said they had been prevented from eavesdropping on the news of the heavens and were now being struck by burning flames. Their people told them: you have only been prevented because of something major that has happened — so go all over the earth, east and west, and see what it is that has obstructed you. So they travelled all over the earth, east and west, searching. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that this blocking began when the Prophet ﷺ was blessed with prophethood, and that a jinn who ventured upward to overhear the heavenly news was chased away by a meteor directed at him.)

A group of them went towards Tihamah, and there they found the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at a place called Nakhlah, along the way to the ʿUkaz market, leading his Companions in the Fajr prayer. When the jinn heard the recitation of the Qur'an they stopped to listen to it, and then they said: "By Allah! This is what has prevented you from eavesdropping on the news of the heavens." Then they returned to their people and told them: "Our people! We certainly have heard an amazing recitation (the Qur'an), it guides to the right path. So we have believed in it, and we will join none in worship with our Lord." Al-Bukhari recorded a similar narration, and Muslim recorded it in this form; At-Tirmidhi also recorded it, as did An-Nasa'i in his *Tafsir*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the human texture: the Arabs used to set up trade fairs on special days in various places for commercial and social purposes, where people of all areas would assemble, set up shops and hold gatherings — much like the exhibitions of our own day. One such fair was held at ʿUkaz, and the Prophet ﷺ was intending to go there, probably for preaching and calling towards Islam. So this was a preaching journey; the audience Allah actually sent him that dawn was one he could not see.

## "They said: Listen quietly"

Ayah 29 says *We sent toward you* — the initiative is Allah's, not theirs. What the jinn did on arrival is the heart of the scene. ʿAbdullah bin Masʿud reported that the jinn came down upon the Prophet ﷺ while he was reciting the Qur'an at a place called Nakhlah, and when they heard him they said *anṣitū* — which, Ibn Kathir explains, means simply: hush. They were nine in number, and one of them was called Zawbaʿah; and it was upon this that ayah 29 and what follows, down to "manifest error," was revealed.

Sit with that. The first act of faith in this story is silence. Not argument, not a question — a group of powerful, ordinarily unruly creatures shushing one another so that no word of the recitation is lost. Ibn Kathir also cites a narration that Imam Ahmad alone recorded, from Az-Zubayr, that this was at Nakhlah while Allah's Messenger was performing the ʿIsha prayer, and that they were as Allah describes in Surat Al-Jinn: *they crowded on top of each other to hear him* (72:19) — Sufyan said, "They stood on top of each other like piled wool." That is the picture: a crush of listeners, packed tight around a man who did not know they were there.

## The Prophet ﷺ did not know they had come

This is one of the most striking details, and Ibn Kathir states it plainly on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas: Allah's Messenger ﷺ never recited Qur'an to the jinn on that occasion, nor did he see them. They only listened to his recitation and went back to their people; he learned of it when Allah revealed to him, *Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of jinn have listened* (72:1). Ibn Kathir notes that what was revealed to him at that point was only the saying of the jinn. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same from Ibn-ul-Mundhir quoting ʿAbdul Malik: the Prophet ﷺ did not become aware of the jinn coming and going, and of their embracing the faith after listening to the Qur'an, until Surat Al-Jinn was revealed and he was informed of the incident.

There is a quiet lesson in that for anyone who recites or teaches. The most consequential fruit of that dawn's recitation was completely invisible to the reciter. Later on, Ibn Kathir says, they came to him in groups, one party after another, and one group after another.

## How many, and how often

The sources record more than one visit, and are careful to say so.

- Ibn Masʿud's report: **nine**, one of them called Zawbaʿah.
- Maʿārif ul Qurʼān mentions another narration that these jinn were inhabitants of Nasibin, **either seven or nine** in number, and that when they told their nation about it and motivated them to embrace faith, **three hundred** of them presented themselves for embracing Islam (Abu Nuʿaim, Al-Waqidi, quoting Kaʿb al-Ahbar, as in *Ruh-ul-Maʿani*).
- Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then resolves the apparent tension: there are diverse narrations in other ahadith too, but since they are about various incidents at different times, there is no contradiction between them. It supports this with a statement of Ibn ʿAbbas reported by Tabarani in *Awsat* and by Ibn Marduwaih that the jinn came to the Prophet ﷺ many times, and it quotes Khafaji's conclusion that the cumulative outcome of the various ahadith is that the jinn presented themselves to him **six times** to benefit from his teachings (*Ruh-ul-Maʿani* and *Bayan-ul-Qurʼan*).

## Warners, not messengers

Ayah 29 ends: *they returned to their people as warners* (mundhirīn). Ibn Kathir explains this simply — they went back to their people and warned them about what they had heard from Allah's Messenger ﷺ — and he compares it to Allah's words about those who gain understanding in religion *and warn their people when they return to them, so that they might be cautious* (9:122).

This ayah, Ibn Kathir says, has been used as evidence that the jinn have **warners from among themselves, but no messengers**. He states there is no doubt that Allah did not send messengers from among the jinn, and gives the evidence:

- *And We did not send before you as Messengers any but men, to whom We revealed, from among the people of cities* (12:109).
- *And We never sent before you any of the Messengers but verily they ate food and walked in the markets* (25:20).
- *And We placed in his descendants prophethood and Scripture* (29:27) — said of Ibrahim (upon him be peace), so that every prophet Allah sent after him was from his offspring and progeny.

The obvious objection is Allah's address in Surat Al-Anʿam, *O company of jinn and human beings! Did there not come to you Messengers from among you?* (6:130). Ibn Kathir answers that it applies to the two kinds **collectively**, but pertains specifically to just one of them — the human. He illustrates with a familiar Qur'anic usage: *From both of them emerge pearl and coral* (55:22) — although Allah said "both of them," this applies to only one of the two types of water.

The distinction matters. A warner is not a bearer of new revelation; a warner is someone who heard the truth and could not keep quiet about it. Which is exactly the role ayat 30–32 show them playing.

## "A Book sent down after Musa" (ayah 30)

The believing jinn open their appeal by placing the Qur'an on the map of revelation: *we have truly heard a Book sent down after Musa, confirming what came before it.* Ibn Kathir explains *confirming what came before it* as the Scriptures that were revealed before it to the previous prophets.

Why say "after Musa" and not "after ʿIsa"? Ibn Kathir's answer: they did not mention ʿIsa (peace be upon him) because the Injil revealed to him contained admonitions and exhortations but very few permissions or prohibitions, so it was in reality like a complement to the legislation of the Tawrah, the Tawrah being the reference. That is why they said, "Sent down after Musa." He notes that Waraqah bin Nawfal spoke in the same way when the Prophet ﷺ told him about his first meeting with Jibril, An-Namus (peace be upon him). Waraqah said: "Very good, very good! This is (the angel) that used to come to Musa. I wish that I was still a young man (to support you)." (The words in brackets are the clarifications supplied in the source itself.)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that some exegetes took the words "after Musa" to indicate that these jinn were Jews, since the Injil revealed to ʿIsa (peace be upon him) after Musa (peace be upon him) is not mentioned — and then rejects the inference: **there is no clear narration to support it**, and their not referring to the Injil cannot be sufficient proof that the jinn were Jews. It offers another possible reason for the omission: the Injil follows the Tawrah in most of its commandments, whereas the Qur'an, like the Tawrah, is an independent Book with different commands, rules and regulations. It is likely, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, that the underlying idea was to state that the Qur'an is a Book independent in the way the Tawrah was.

## Truth, and the straight path

Then they say it *guides to the truth and to the straight path* — and Ibn Kathir shows that this is not one praise repeated twice:

- **"It guides to the truth"** — meaning, in belief and information.
- **"and to the straight path"** — meaning, in deeds.

For, as Ibn Kathir puts it, the Qur'an contains two things: information and commandments. Its information is true, and its commandments are all just — as Allah says, *And the Word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and in justice* (6:115). He sets the same pair alongside *It is He Who has sent His Messenger with the guidance and the religion of truth* (48:28), where the guidance is beneficent knowledge and the religion of truth means righteous good deeds.

So a single night's listening gave these jinn an accurate summary of what the Qur'an is: news you can trust, and a road you can walk.

## "Respond to Allah's caller" (ayah 31)

Now the appeal turns urgent: *O our people! Respond to Allah's caller, and believe in him.* Ibn Kathir draws a major conclusion from this: it is proof that Muhammad ﷺ has been sent to both human beings **and** jinn. The jinn who heard him understood at once that his call included them.

Then the promise: *He will forgive you some of your sins, and protect you from a painful torment.* The Arabic is *yaghfir lakum min dhunūbikum*, and the little word *min* ("of / some of") has been read two ways:

- **Some scholars** say that "some" here is auxiliary — an extra word carrying no additional meaning in Arabic idiom — so the sense is simply "He will forgive you your sins." Ibn Kathir mentions this view but calls it questionable, since it is rarely used that way to strengthen an affirmative meaning. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that on this reading — *min* as an extra word — no explanation is required.
- **Others** say it means partial forgiveness. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān spells out what that would mean: that "some sins" will be forgiven by embracing Islam, which would indicate that only sins relating to the rights of Allah are forgiven, and not the rights owed to people.

Both readings are held by respected exegetes. Either way, the second half of the promise is unqualified: *and protect you from a painful torment* — meaning, in Ibn Kathir's words, He will protect you from His painful punishment.

## Nowhere left to run (ayah 32)

The sermon closes with the other side of the appeal:

- *whoever does not respond to Allah's caller cannot escape on earth* — meaning, in Ibn Kathir's words, that Allah's power encompasses him and surrounds him. There is no patch of the earth outside it.
- *and he will not have besides Allah any protectors* — meaning, no one can protect him against Allah.
- *Those are in manifest error* — Ibn Kathir says plainly: this is a threat and warning.

So those jinn called their people with encouragement and warning — mercy held out in ayah 31, consequence spelled out in ayah 32. And it bore fruit: Ibn Kathir concludes that because of this, many of the jinn took heed and came to Allah's Messenger ﷺ in successive delegations — "and verily, Allah is worthy of all praise and gratitude, and Allah knows best."

## Living it

Three things this passage asks of a believer, and none of them require adding anything to it.

**Listen the way they listened.** *Anṣitū* — hush. They did not talk over the recitation, and they did not treat it as background noise. One attentive hearing changed their nation's history.

**Do not sit on what you heard.** The moment the recitation ended they *turned back to their people*. Ibn Kathir's comparison with 9:122 makes the pattern explicit: understand, then return and warn your own. Notice who they addressed — *yā qawmanā*, "O our people." Their first audience was their own community.

**Notice the shame in the comparison.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's framing is the sting of the passage: unseen creatures, prouder and haughtier than the Makkans, had their hearts softened after hearing the Qur'an. A reader who has the Qur'an in his hands daily, and remains unmoved, is the one this passage is really aimed at.

passages.title: Power to raise the dead, and the call to patience
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat close Sūrat al-Aḥqāf. They move in one unbroken line: first an argument that the Allah who created the heavens and the earth can certainly give life to the dead (ayah 33), then a scene showing the deniers set before the Fire and admitting the truth (ayah 34), and finally a command to the Prophet ﷺ to be patient and not to hurry the punishment along (ayah 35). What holds them together is a single logic: *the resurrection is real, so the believer's job is to wait well.*

## Ayah 33: the argument you can see with your own eyes

The ayah opens with a question that is really a rebuke: **"Do they not see...?"** Ibn Kathir tells us exactly who is being addressed — those who deny resurrection on the Day of Judgment and doubt that the bodies will be raised on that Last Day. Allah does not answer their doubt with an abstract proof. He points them at the sky and the ground under their feet.

The key phrase is **وَلَمْ يَعْيَ بِخَلْقِهِنَّ** — "and was not wearied by their creation." Ibn Kathir explains it plainly: the creation of the heavens and the earth did not exhaust Him. Rather, He commanded them, *"Be,"* and they were, without any refusal or delay. They obeyed and responded to Him with submission and fear.

Sit with that for a moment, because the whole argument rests on it. A human builder is drained by his building; the bigger the work, the more it costs him. So people instinctively imagine that re-assembling scattered bodies must be an enormous, perhaps impossible, undertaking. The ayah dismantles the instinct from both ends. Allah's creating is not a labour that depletes Him at all — it is a word, and the thing exists. And the thing He created that way is vastly larger than a human body. Ibn Kathir brings the verse that states this directly:

> "Verily, the creation of the heavens and earth is greater than the creation of the people. But most people do not know." (40:57)

So the question answers itself, as Ibn Kathir puts it: **Is He not then able to revive the dead?**

Notice that Allah does not leave the question hanging for the reader to resolve. Ibn Kathir points out that Allah responds to His own question:

> **"Yes, He surely is Able to do all things."**

That word "Yes" — *balā* — is worth holding on to. It comes back in the very next ayah, in a very different mouth.

## Ayah 34: the confession at the edge of the Fire

Ibn Kathir reads this ayah as a threat and a warning to whoever disbelieves in Allah. The scene is stark: **"on the Day when those who disbelieve will be exposed to the Fire."** There is nothing left to argue with; the thing they rejected is set right before them.

And then the question: **"Is this not the truth?"** Ibn Kathir unpacks the tone behind it — it will be said to them, *"Isn't this the truth? Is this magic, or do you not see?"* That is not a neutral question. The Fire itself is put to the test: *look at it; is it magic? are your eyes failing you?*

Their answer: **"Yes, by our Lord!"** — the same word *balā* that answered the question in ayah 33 is now spoken by the deniers about the Fire. Ibn Kathir's comment is one line and it says everything: **they will have no choice but to confess.** And they swear on it — *by our Lord* — by the very Lord they would not affirm when affirming was free and belief was a choice.

There is a hard mercy in seeing this now. The confession will come either way. The only question is whether a person makes it in this life, when making it means something, or on that Day, when it changes nothing.

The reply they receive is the last word of the exchange: **"Then taste the torment, because you used to disbelieve!"** The punishment is not arbitrary — the ayah itself ties it to what they used to do: a settled, ongoing rejection. That link between deed and consequence is picked up again at the very end of ayah 35.

## Ayah 35: "So be patient, as the Messengers of firm resolve were patient"

Having established the Day, Allah turns to His Messenger ﷺ. Ibn Kathir frames the shift: Allah commands His Messenger ﷺ to observe patience with those among his people who rejected him — patient **"as they were patient with their people's rejection of them."**

This is one of the most consoling instructions in the Qur'an, because of *how* it consoles. It does not tell the Prophet ﷺ that the pain is small, or that the rejection is imaginary. It hands him a lineage. You are not the first; you are the latest in a line of men who stood before hostile peoples and held.

### Who are "those of firm resolve" (أُولُو الْعَزْمِ)?

Here the two commentaries in front of us give complementary depth, and it is worth taking them in turn.

**Ibn Kathir** names them: *"Those of determination"* among the Messengers are Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, ʿIsa, and the last of all of the Prophets, Muhammad ﷺ. He grounds the list textually: Allah has specifically mentioned their names in two ayat — Sūrat al-Aḥzāb (33:7) and Sūrat ash-Shūrā (42:13).

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** raises a grammatical question that changes how the phrase reads. The Arabic is *ūlū al-ʿazmi **min** ar-rusul.* Ordinarily the word **مِنْ (min)** gives the sense of "some" — which would make the phrase "those of resolve *from among* the Messengers," implying a select subgroup. But according to the authentic exegetes, Maʿārif says, *min* here is **not** in the sense of "some." It is rather for *bayān* — "description," to use the grammatical term. On that reading the sense is: **all messengers are resolute people.** Resolve is not a distinction some prophets earned; it is what being a messenger means.

(This is a good place to notice how much a single small word can carry. Maʿārif discusses this same word *min* elsewhere, at the phrase "will forgive your sins for you" — there, taken in the sense of "some," it would mean that some sins are forgiven by embracing Islam, indicating that sins relating to the rights of Allah are forgiven but not the rights of people; while some exegetes take *min* there as an extra word carrying no additional meaning in Arabic idiom, on which reading no explanation is required. Same two-letter word, and the sense of the sentence turns on which way you read it.)

Maʿārif then holds two truths together rather than choosing between them. All messengers are resolute — *and* variation in the grades of qualities between messengers is proved from the Qur'an itself:

> "Those are the messengers, some of whom We have given excellence over some others." (2:253)

So those prophets who excel other prophets in the quality of being resolute and courageous have been given this title in a special way. Maʿārif is careful to record that **there are differences of opinion as to who they are**, and states the majority position: this special title is given to the prophets mentioned in Sūrat al-Aḥzāb 7 — *"And (recall) when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you and from Nuh and Ibrahim and Musa and ʿIsa, the son of Maryam. And We did take from them a firm covenant."* That majority list matches Ibn Kathir's exactly.

### What resolve cost the Prophet ﷺ

Sayyidah ʿĀʾishah ؓ states that the Prophet ﷺ said that the delights, luxuries and pleasures of this world do not befit Muhammad ﷺ and his family, because Allah does not accept anything less than patience from those who are "resolute," and he ﷺ had received this divine order: *"So, O Prophet, observe patience, as the resolute messengers observed patience."*

That report is worth reading twice. The Prophet ﷺ treated ayah 35 not as a general encouragement but as a command addressed to him — one that shaped the standard of living of his own household. Being counted among the resolute was not, in his eyes, an honorific. It was a demand.

### "And be in no hurry for them"

The second half of the command is as important as the first: **وَلَا تَسْتَعْجِلْ لَهُمْ.** Ibn Kathir explains it precisely — *do not rush the punishment for them.*

This is a subtle spiritual correction. When you are wronged persistently and you cannot stop it, the heart's natural escape is to demand that the wrongdoing be ended *now* — that judgment fall today. The ayah closes that exit and replaces it with patience. Ibn Kathir cites two verses where Allah gives a similar instruction:

> "And leave Me alone to deal with the rejectors, those who are in possession of good things of life. And give them respite for a little while." (73:11)

> "So allow time for the disbelievers, and leave them for a while." (86:17)

In each, the reckoning is not cancelled — it is **kept**, and kept by Allah Himself. "Leave Me alone to deal with them" is not a denial of justice; it is a statement of who carries it. The believer's part is the waiting; the settling belongs to Allah.

### The hour that swallows a lifetime

Then comes the line that makes the patience bearable: **"On the Day when they will see what they are promised, it will be as though they had not remained (in the world) except an hour in a day."**

Whatever respite the deniers are given — decades of comfort, a whole life of it — will feel, at the moment the promise arrives, like a single hour snatched out of one afternoon. Ibn Kathir sets two other verses beside it to let the point land:

> "On the Day they see it (the Hour), it will be as though they had not remained (in the world) except for a day's afternoon or its morning." (79:46)

> "And on the Day when He shall gather them together, (it will be) as if they had not stayed but an hour of a day. They will recognize each other." (10:45)

Notice what this does to the command that precedes it. *Do not rush them* is easier to obey once you see that the delay you are being asked to endure is, measured against the reality it opens onto, almost nothing. The respite that looks so long and so unfair from inside history collapses to an hour the moment history ends.

### "A clear message"

**بَلَاغٌ** — Ibn Kathir's gloss is brief: **this Qur'an provides a clear concept.** That single word quietly closes the sūrah's argument: what needed to be conveyed has been conveyed, and conveyed clearly.

### "But will any be destroyed except the defiantly rebellious people?"

The last line of the sūrah is a question with only one possible answer, and it is a statement about Allah's justice. Ibn Kathir: **Allah does not destroy anyone except those who choose the way of destruction.** It is part of Allah's justice that He does not punish anyone except those who deserve the punishment — *and Allah knows best.*

Ruin, on this reading, is never something that ambushes a person. It is chosen.

And so the sūrah ends by answering the fear its own warnings raise. If Allah is this powerful, who is safe? The answer: everyone except those who choose the way of destruction.

## Living it

Three things this passage asks of a believer, in the order it asks them:

**Let creation argue for the resurrection.** The doubt Ibn Kathir describes is a doubt that *bodies* will be raised. Ayah 33 answers it by scale: the heavens and the earth are the greater creation, and making them did not exhaust Him.

**Say "yes" now.** Ayah 34 shows a confession made when there is no choice left. Faith is simply making it while making it still counts.

**Be patient the way the resolute were patient, and do not demand the reckoning early.** Ayah 35 gives the model (Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, ʿIsa, and Muhammad ﷺ — patient under their peoples' rejection), the restraint (*do not rush the punishment for them*), and the reason it is possible (the whole span of waiting will look like an hour of one day). If Allah did not accept less than patience from His most beloved, patience is not the lowest bar for the rest of us — it is the bar.

*This concludes the explanation of Sūrat al-Aḥqāf. And all praise and blessings are due to Allah; both success and protection from faults are by His help.*
